craft_claim: Uplift that denies, minimizes, or invalidates negative emotion can backfire, and the harm is greatest for readers with low self-esteem, so the inspirational voice must not overwrite distress.

supporting_evidence.note: Low-self-esteem participants who repeated a positive self-statement or focused on its truth felt worse than controls, while high-self-esteem participants improved only to a limited degree; the authors conclude positive self-statements may backfire for those who most need them.

supporting_evidence.location: Anxiety, Stress & Coping 36(2):214-228, daily diary analyses
supporting_evidence.note: Higher perceived emotion invalidation predicted lower momentary positive affect and, for high-invalidation individuals, greater negative affect alongside more intense social stress.
The article analyzes toxic positivity as an epistemic wrong in which a person's emotional testimony is dismissed or overridden by mandated cheerfulness.

counterevidence.note: Section G records that high-self-esteem participants improved 'to a limited degree' and that the harm was confined to low-self-esteem participants repeating a positive self-statement in the laboratory, so the backfire is bounded rather than general and does not attach to every uplift voiced over distress.

scope: Any direct address of the reader's distress, failure, or grief.
exceptions: Ritual or ceremonial settings where a shared upbeat register is an agreed convention and no disclosure of distress is at issue.
